body.text: How It All Began

Overdose, abbreviated od, strictly translated as excessive dose, means an overdose and carries no implication of drug abuse; drug abuse is Drug abuse. od is genuinely contained within drug abuse, and drug abuse is colloquially called 'taking'.

The Chinese word for narcotics is a noun peculiar to that language, and is not equivalent to the English Drug. That word refers to highly threatening psychoactive substances; 'Drug' refers to any medicine at large. In English, when describing what Chinese calls narcotics, one doesn't use Medicine or Medication but Drug — and that stereotype has been passed on ever since.

So the first thing is to separate the words: od ≠ abuse ≠ using. Lumping them together makes a fuss over nothing and turns an originally simple problem into a thorny one. Separating them isn't for shelter; it's for being able to handle it.
Basic Mechanism Overview

The gastrointestinal tract absorbs the drug into the blood; the liver transforms (metabolizes) the chemicals in the blood — quite a few drugs only act after metabolism, and the more elaborate the metabolism the more the liver suffers; the kidneys filter unwanted chemicals into primary urine and out — the stranger the drug molecule the more the kidneys suffer. Most od drugs act on the nervous system or the brain.

Drugs are made into different dosage forms: tablets, injections, inhaled gases. A tablet with only one ingredient is a single-ingredient preparation; with several, a compound preparation. To change physical properties, drugs are often paired with an acid or a base (dextromethorphan hydrobromide, amantadine hydrochloride...); when naming a drug the acid or base is usually left out — one says amantadine, not amantadine hydrochloride.
The half-life is the period needed for half the drug to leave the body after dosing; different dosage forms have different half-lives.
Receptors: Key and Lock

Chemicals bind to receptors the way a key is inserted into a keyhole. Neurotransmitters bind to their corresponding receptors and always agonize them; other chemicals (such as drugs) can also bind, but don't always agonize.

Agonism = inserting a matching key and turning the lock open; inverse agonism = inserting a key and wrecking the keyhole; antagonism = inserting a non-matching key and blocking the keyhole; blockade = taping over the keyhole. Different actions on different receptors produce different drug effects.
Main neurotransmitters: dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin (5-HT), glutamate, acetylcholine, GABA, endorphins, Substance P. The first three are together called monoamines.
Effects and Side Effects

Drug effects divide into main effects and side effects, and the division is artificial and changes with circumstances: for treating mania, quetiapine's drowsiness is a side effect; for treating insomnia it's the main effect. They also divide into acute and chronic: under inappropriate use, one dose of a benzodiazepine brings short-term sleep but adds up into long-term insomnia; od on dextro causes acute dissociation and leaves chronic dissociation behind.

A side effect that damages the body under given circumstances is called toxicity (hepatotoxicity, neurotoxicity and so on). Low-dose atropine can be a muscle relaxant; an overdose can be a nerve poison. Low-dose paracetamol is a cold medicine; a high dose is hepatotoxic.

Psychoactive effects overview: dissociation, SRI, antidepressant, stimulation, delirium, sedation, hypnosis, opioid anesthesia, hallucination, social enhancement, anti-dissociation; the main effects are changes to personality, mood and cognition, plus amnesia. Side effects overview: schizophrenia, dissociative disorder, depersonalization, Alzheimer's, depression, mania, bipolar, anxiety, toxicity, lowered intelligence/memory/cognition, withdrawal reactions, opioid addiction; acute ones include serotonin syndrome, anticholinergic syndrome, disorientation and so on. Physiological side effects overview: headache, organ damage, gastric ulcer, nerve/brain damage, vomiting, respiratory depression, seizures and so on.
Schizophrenia ≠ depersonalization disorder ≠ multiple personality disorder. The three are different illnesses with different symptoms.
The First Line of Caution
*Sertraline can't be o'd.*

So many people asked this back then. SSRIs like sertraline basically have no psychoactive effect and an overdose easily triggers serotonin syndrome, so they have no 'OD value' — a typical case of knowledge doing harm reduction: telling people who don't know this piece of common sense is entirely agreeable.

The introduction ends here. It gives you words, gives you mechanism, gives you the first line of common sense; it doesn't give you doses, formulas or sources. For the rest, go to the effect entries and the specific entries, and go to the people in the reports who lived.
